"Below are questions proposed for a research problem, each with the reframing behind it. Classify each one.
kind: \"reframe\" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before; \"copies\" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side; \"other\" otherwise.
meets_criterion: \"yes\" or \"no\" for this criterion: none given; answer NA
Give for each a quote from the proposal and a reason of at most 25 words. Decide only from the text below; do not use tools.
Problem:
**IC-V1 · Force-field error floor for coolant MD: an enlarged C10–C50 benchmark scored against measurement.** seed pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: not the lever · PASS

**Question.** Will graphics-card molecular simulations using Green–Kubo on C10–C50 hydrocarbons and esters rank immersion coolants' viscosity and thermal conductivity the same way measurements do?

**What is known.** Ogbomo and colleagues, in 2026, used Green–Kubo molecular dynamics to compute viscosity and thermal conductivity for eight C10–C50 molecules at 40 °C and compared with measurements [s_ogbomo_md]. Whether the error is a correctable bias or a random floor that caps ranking, and how rank agreement holds over hundreds of molecules [s_ogbomo_db].

**Hypothesis.** Green–Kubo MD with one fixed force field has a chemistry-dependent error floor near 25 percent that more molecules cannot remove [s_ogbomo_res].

**If compute is the lever.** At 120 molecules, held-out viscosity error after bias correction falls below 15 percent and rank correlation with measurement exceeds 0.9 [s_ogbomo_res].

**If not.** Held-out viscosity error stays above 25 percent and rank correlation below 0.7 at every set size, capping candidate ranking [s_ogbomo_res].

**Test.** One LAMMPS LOPLS-AA Green–Kubo protocol at 40 °C, six five-nanosecond replicas per molecule, run on 8, 24, 48 then 120 molecules from the public 835-molecule reference set, scored only against measured viscosity and thermal conductivity [s_ogbomo_db].

*Compute axis.* Benchmark molecules scored against measured viscosity and thermal conductivity: 8–120 molecules, 4 levels. Closest prior: 8 [s_ogbomo_md], beyond it.

*Restructuring.* none.

**Check first.** Repeat the published eight-molecule Green–Kubo run first: density within 4% for seven molecules and thermal conductivity over-predicted for all eight [s_ogbomo_res]. Tolerance: same bias signs for viscosity and thermal conductivity; density error within 4 percentage points of the published error; per-molecule viscosity within 20% of the reference value.

**Would not show.** Shows transport-property error only at 40 °C for pure liquids between 1 and 50 mPa·s, not blends or sold coolants. Cannot show ranking behaviour beyond 120 molecules.

*Cost.* Plans $940.98 of the $1,000 budget over 59 machine-hours, leaving $59.02. Main guess: assumed MD throughput per GPU [p], measured after $36.20 of spend; the budget is reached if it is 1.1× lower. 3 cost flags in the block.
Proposals: [{\"index\":1,\"bottleneck\":\"The ~25% floor is stated for absolute per-molecule properties, so the 8→24→48→120 ladder mostly re-measures the same floor with more precision; the quantity the pipeline actually needs — which of two candidates ranks higher — is never measured directly.\",\"assumption\":\"That ranking accuracy is capped by absolute accuracy, i.e. that force-field errors are independent across molecules. Same-chemistry molecules share the same parameter bias, so errors are correlated and largely cancel inside a difference.\",\"reframe\":\"Change the objective and the unit of work: from the absolute property of one molecule to the sign of the difference within a pair. Score pairwise ordering accuracy and spend simulation only on pairs the current ranking leaves ambiguous.\",\"question\":\"For molecule pairs whose measured viscosities differ by at least 10%, what fraction are ordered the same way by the published Green–Kubo runs — and does that fraction stay at or above 0.9 while absolute per-molecule error stays near 25%?\",\"measure\":\"Re-score the published 8-molecule table as 28 pairs (sign agreement for viscosity and for thermal conductivity); no new simulation, roughly an afternoon of analysis, under $10. If too few pairs clear the 10% separation, add the next 16 molecules (about $125 at the plan's ~$7.8 per molecule) and repeat.\",\"compute_after\":\"If sign accuracy is high, the 120-molecule absolute-error campaign and the 15% error target can be dropped; compute moves to targeted paired runs near decision boundaries, with many candidate pairs run side by side.\",\"exact\":\"fraction f of pairs (A,B) with |eta_meas(A)-eta_meas(B)|/eta_meas >= 0.10 for which sign[eta_MD(A)-eta_MD(B)] = sign[eta_meas(A)-eta_meas(B)]; the same quantity for thermal conductivity.\",\"expected\":\"f >= 0.9 for both properties despite ~25% absolute error, because the shared chemistry bias appears in both members of a pair and cancels in the difference.\",\"fails_if\":\"f <= 0.7, meaning the error is dominated by molecule-specific, uncorrelated noise; differences then inherit the full floor and ranking really is capped — the reframe buys nothing.\",\"closest_prior\":\"The published 8-molecule benchmark [s_ogbomo_md] reports only per-molecule absolute errors; this re-scores the identical data as 28 pairwise decisions — beyond it at zero simulation cost.\"},{\"index\":2,\"bottleneck\":\"With LOPLS-AA parameters fixed, no amount of Green–Kubo sampling lowers the error floor: molecules 9–120 only estimate the same floor more precisely. The published result that all eight thermal conductivities are over-predicted points to a shared, parameter-level bias rather than random per-molecule error.\",\"assumption\":\"That the force field is an untouchable input and error can only be corrected after the fact (the plan's output bias correction). The floor is treated as a fact of nature instead of as one or two mis-set parameters.\",\"reframe\":\"Change the order of steps: before adding molecules, make the force field itself the object of compute — a small scaling sweep of the one or two Lennard-Jones or charge parameters plausibly carrying the bias, fit on the 8 known molecules, frozen, then tested on the next 8.\",\"question\":\"Does a single global rescaling of one parameter class (for example the ester carbonyl LJ epsilon, or the united-atom CHx epsilon), fit to the 8 published viscosities, cut held-out viscosity error on 8 unseen molecules below 15%?\",\"measure\":\"Kill-signal sweep: 5 epsilon-scale values x 8 molecules x one 2-ns run each = 80 ns, about $25 at the plan's ~$0.26/ns. Only if training error collapses monotonically, run the frozen setting on 8 new molecules with the full 6x5 ns protocol (240 ns, about $65). Total about $90.\",\"compute_after\":\"If the refit transfers, compute buys depth instead of breadth: per-chemistry-class refits, then a corrected-field screen of the full 835-molecule set at a lower floor — more compute now changes the answer rather than re-measuring it.\",\"exact\":\"held-out mean absolute percent error of Green–Kubo viscosity at 40 °C on 8 molecules excluded from the fit, using one frozen global scaling; secondary: the same for thermal conductivity.\",\"expected\":\"Because all 8 conductivities were over-predicted (one shared sign), a single knob removes most of the bias; held-out viscosity error lands at 12–18%.\",\"fails_if\":\"Best-fit training error stays above 20%, or the optimal scaling reverses sign between hydrocarbons and esters — then the error is molecule-specific, not parameter-level, and refitting merely overfits the eight.\",\"closest_prior\":\"The published benchmark [s_ogbomo_md] holds the field fixed and only reports the bias; the plan corrects outputs afterward. Fitting the field against the same measurements is the step beyond both.\"},{\"index\":3,\"bottleneck\":\"The unit of work is a pure liquid, but the pipeline's product is a formulated single-phase coolant, usually a blend; the plan itself concedes it cannot show blends, so no amount of pure-molecule compute at 40 °C answers whether blend rankings are right.\",\"assumption\":\"That pure-component rankings transfer to blends through an implicit mixing rule — that mixing adds no new error beyond the per-component floor.\",\"reframe\":\"Change the unit of work from molecule to mixture: simulate the blend directly at several compositions, so compute acts on the object actually being ranked and measures whether mixing itself is predictable.\",\"question\":\"For one binary pair from the benchmark set at three compositions (25/50/75 mol%), does direct blend simulation reproduce the measured blend viscosity within the same error band as the pure components, and does a mole-fraction mixing rule built from the already-simulated pures do measurably worse?\",\"measure\":\"3 compositions x 6 replicas x 5 ns = 90 ns, about $25, using published blend data for the same pair; compare direct-blend error against the mixing-rule prediction from the existing pure simulations. Total about $25–50.\",\"compute_after\":\"If direct-blend error tracks the pure-component floor, the search space opens up: compute screens blend compositions of a few validated components (combinatorially many liquids from few chemistries), and pure-molecule runs shrink to calibration.\",\"exact\":\"mean absolute percent error versus measurement of Green–Kubo blend viscosity at 40 °C at mole fractions 0.25/0.50/0.75, compared against the mixing-rule prediction built from the two pure simulations.\",\"expected\":\"Direct-blend error within roughly 5 points of the pure-component floor; the mixing rule biased by more than that for ester–hydrocarbon pairs, so direct simulation wins on ranking.\",\"fails_if\":\"Blend error exceeds the pure floor by more than a factor of 2, or the ordering across compositions is wrong while pure ordering is right — blend MD then carries its own uncharacterized error that must be fixed before the reframe is usable.\",\"closest_prior\":\"The 8-molecule pure-liquid benchmark and the 835-molecule reference set [s_ogbomo_md, s_ogbomo_db] contain no mixtures; even one binary composition series is beyond both.\"}]

Return only one JSON value, with no other text, that matches this JSON Schema:

Let me analyze each proposal carefully.

The classification criteria:
- "reframe" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before
- "copies" if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side
- "other" otherwise

meets_criterion: "yes" or "no" for this criterion: none given; answer NA

So for all items, meets_criterion should be "NA" since no criterion was given.

Wait, let me re-read: "meets_criterion: \"yes\" or \"no\" for this criterion: none given; answer NA"

The criterion section says "none given; answer NA" — so all items get meets_criterion: "NA".

Now classify each:

**Proposal 1:**
The reframe: "Change the objective and the unit of work: from the absolute property of one molecule to the sign of the difference within a pair. Score pairwise ordering accuracy and spend simulation only on pairs the current ranking leaves ambiguous."

This changes what is measured — from absolute per-molecule error to pairwise sign agreement. This is a change in what is computed/measured so more compute buys something it did not before (targeted paired runs near decision boundaries). However, there's a subtlety: the initial step is re-scoring existing data (no new compute), and "compute_after" says if sign accuracy is high, compute moves to targeted paired runs — "with many candidate pairs run side by side". Hmm, "run side by side" — is that copies? The key is that the reframe changes what is computed (pairwise ordering accuracy vs absolute per-molecule error). The objective changes from absolute property to sign of difference within a pair. That's a change in what is measured. So kind: "reframe".

But wait — the compute_after says "compute moves to targeted paired runs near decision boundaries, with many candidate pairs run side by side." Running pairs side by side could be seen as "copies" (running same computation on more items side by side). But the primary classification is about the reframe itself: it changes the objective and unit of work from absolute per-molecule property to pairwise sign. That's clearly changing what is computed/measured. The measurement "fraction f of pairs ... for which sign matches" is a new measurement. So "reframe".

**Proposal 2:**
The reframe: "Change the order of steps: before adding molecules, make the force field itself the object of compute — a small scaling sweep of the one or two Lennard-Jones or charge parameters plausibly carrying the bias, fit on the 8 known molecules, frozen, then tested on the next 8."

This changes what is computed — the force field parameters become the object of compute rather than adding molecules. More compute now "changes the answer rather than re-measuring it" (compute_after). This is clearly a reframe: changes what is computed so more compute buys something new. kind: "reframe".

**Proposal 3:**
The reframe: "Change the unit of work from molecule to mixture: simulate the blend directly at several compositions, so compute acts on the object actually being ranked and measures whether mixing itself is predictable."

This changes the unit of work from molecule to mixture — computing something new (blend simulations). This is a change in what is computed. More compute buys the ability to screen blend compositions combinatorially. kind: "reframe".

Hmm, but let me double check each one more carefully against the "copies" definition: "if it only runs the same computation more times, on more items, or side by side."

Proposal 1: The re-scoring of published data is analysis, not new compute. But the question is about the proposal's kind. The proposal changes what is measured (pairwise sign agreement vs absolute error). The compute_after involves targeted paired runs — running simulations on pairs, which is different from absolute-error campaigns. The key change: the objective and unit of work change. This is a reframe.

Actually wait — let me reconsider. The pairwise sign agreement is derived from the same MD simulations. Running "many candidate pairs side by side" — the simulations themselves are the same Green-Kubo MD runs, just used differently. But the measured quantity changes (sign of difference vs absolute property), and the ordering/scoring changes. The definition of "reframe" is "if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before". The pairwise ordering accuracy is a new measured quantity. Targeted compute on ambiguous pairs buys ranking accuracy that absolute-error compute did not buy. So yes, reframe.

Proposal 2: The force field becomes the object of compute — a parameter sweep. This is definitely new computation (different parameter values, fitting). Reframe.

Proposal 3: The unit of work changes from molecule to mixture — blend simulation is a different computation. Reframe.

All three seem to be "reframe". Let me sanity check whether any could be "copies" or "other".

Proposal 1's compute_after: "compute moves to targeted paired runs near decision boundaries, with many candidate pairs run side by side." If sign accuracy is high, drop the 120-molecule campaign. The pairs are new items (pairs vs single molecules), and the measurement is pairwise ordering. The essential claim: errors correlate and cancel in differences — measuring something new (sign accuracy). It changes what is measured. Reframe.

Proposal 2: Parameter sweep, fitting the force field. Definitely changes what is computed. Reframe.

Proposal 3: Blend simulation at compositions. Definitely changes what is computed (mixtures vs pures). Reframe.

Hmm, is it plausible that all three are reframes? The problem statement says the plan expects "not the lever" — i.e., the original plan (more molecules) is the "copies" style: running the same computation on more items (8→24→48→120 molecules). The proposals are reframings of that. Each proposal changes what is computed/measured:
1. Pairwise sign agreement instead of absolute error.
2. Force-field parameter fitting instead of adding molecules.
3. Blend simulation instead of pure-molecule simulation.

All three are genuine reframes. None are merely "copies" (running same computation more times). None are "other".

Actually, let me reconsider proposal 1 more carefully. Is re-scoring published data as pairs a change in what is computed? The exact measure: "fraction f of pairs (A,B) with |eta_meas(A)-eta_meas(B)|/eta_meas >= 0.10 for which sign[eta_MD(A)-eta_MD(B)] = sign[eta_meas(A)-eta_meas(B)]". This is a new statistic computed from existing data. And the compute_after: "If sign accuracy is high, the 120-molecule absolute-error campaign and the 15% error target can be dropped; compute moves to targeted paired runs near decision boundaries, with many candidate pairs run side by side."

The reframe changes what is measured (ordering accuracy vs absolute error) and what compute buys (targeted ambiguity resolution vs floor re-measurement). Yes, reframe.

Now meets_criterion: "yes" or "no" for this criterion: none given; answer NA. So all: "NA".

Quotes — pick a representative quote from each proposal, likely from the "reframe" field:

1. "Change the objective and the unit of work: from the absolute property of one molecule to the sign of the difference within a pair."
2. "Change the order of steps: before adding molecules, make the force field itself the object of compute"
3. "Change the unit of work from molecule to mixture: simulate the blend directly at several compositions"

Reasons (at most 25 words):

1. "Shifts the measured quantity from absolute per-molecule error to pairwise sign agreement; compute then targets ambiguous pairs instead of re-measuring the floor." — count words: Shifts(1) the(2) measured(3) quantity(4) from(5) absolute(6) per-molecule(7) error(8) to(9) pairwise(10) sign(11) agreement;(12) compute(13) then(14) targets(15) ambiguous(16) pairs(17) instead(18) of(19) re-measuring(20) the(21) floor(22). 22 words. Good.

2. "Makes force-field parameters the object of compute; more compute buys bias removal and a lower floor, not just re-measurement." — Makes(1) force-field(2) parameters(3) the(4) object(5) of(6) compute;(7) more(8) compute(9) buys(10) bias(11) removal(12) and(13) a(14) lower(15) floor,(16) not(17) just(18) re-measurement(19). 19 words. Good.

3. "Changes the computed object from pure molecules to blends at compositions; compute then buys combinatorial blend screening, not more pure runs." — Changes(1) the(2) computed(3) object(4) from(5) pure(6) molecules(7) to(8) blends(9) at(10) compositions;(11) compute(12) then(13) buys(14) combinatorial(15) blend(16) screening,(17) not(18) more(19) pure(20) runs(21). 21 words. Good.

Now, one more consideration on proposal 1: could it be "copies"? The compute_after mentions "many candidate pairs run side by side" — side by side is in the copies definition. But the classification is about the proposal's main thrust: it changes what is measured (pairwise ordering accuracy). The targeted runs on ambiguous pairs are not "the same computation more times on more items" — they're directed at a new objective. Hmm, actually the pairwise runs are still Green-Kubo MD simulations on molecules — the same computation — but the scoring and selection of what to run changes. The question is whether "changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before" fits.

I'd say yes: the measured quantity changes (pairwise sign accuracy, not absolute error), and compute is spent selectively on ambiguous pairs, buying ranking decisions it didn't before. So reframe.

Alternatively, one might argue the pair simulations are the same computation run on pairs (i.e., on more items side by side) — copies. But the proposal's core is the re-scoring as pairwise decisions — a new measurement — and targeted allocation of compute. The "so that more compute buys something it did not before" clause: compute on ambiguous pairs buys ranking accuracy. I'll go with reframe.

For proposal 2, definitely reframe.

For proposal 3, definitely reframe — blend simulation is a different computation than pure-component simulation.

Let me also double-check "other" possibilities. "Other" would be proposals that neither reframe nor copy — e.g., purely analysis, no compute, or something else. Proposal 1's first step is pure analysis of existing data (no new simulation). But the proposal includes compute usage afterward (targeted paired runs, adding 16 molecules). The reframe field explicitly changes the objective and unit of work. The question asks whether pairwise ordering holds — a new measured quantity. I think reframe is right. Even if one could argue "other" for the analysis-only part, the proposal as a whole changes what is measured, and compute_after explicitly redeploys compute. The classification should be based on the proposal's kind as a whole.

Hmm, but wait — let me reconsider. The instruction: "kind: \"reframe\" if it changes what is computed, measured or ordered so that more compute buys something it did not before". For proposal 1: does more compute buy something new? The compute_after says: "compute moves to targeted paired runs near decision boundaries, with many candidate pairs run side by side." So more compute buys resolution of ambiguous pairs — ranking decisions. Previously, more compute only re-measured the absolute floor. So yes, more compute buys something new (ambiguity resolution). Reframe.

For proposal 2: "compute buys depth instead of breadth: per-chemistry-class refits, then a corrected-field screen of the full 835-molecule set at a lower floor — more compute now changes the answer rather than re-measuring it." Explicitly states more compute changes the answer. Reframe.

For proposal 3: "compute screens blend compositions of a few validated components (combinatorially many liquids from few chemistries), and pure-molecule runs shrink to calibration." More compute buys combinatorial blend screening. Reframe.

All three are reframes. All meets_criterion: NA.

Quotes — should be from the proposal text. Let me pick:

1. Quote: "Change the objective and the unit of work: from the absolute property of one molecule to the sign of the difference within a pair. Score pairwise ordering accuracy and spend simulation only on pairs the current ranking leaves ambiguous."

Maybe shorten: "Change the objective and the unit of work: from the absolute property of one molecule to the sign of the difference within a pair."

Or: "make the force field itself the object of compute"

3. Quote: "Change the unit of work from molecule to mixture: simulate the blend directly at several compositions, so compute acts on the object actually being ranked"
